title: Five eras of UX design and the lessons to keep in the AI era
text:
Five eras of UX design and the lessons to keep in the AI era

Human factors has reinvented itself every decade since Bell Labs, the oldest lessons are the ones pointing the way forward.

User Experience did not begin with Don Norman’s job title at Apple. The work is older than the name, and most of it is older than anyone teaching it.

You can earn a degree in this field and never hear about John Karlin shaping telephones at Bell Labs in the 1940s, the principles and laws we follow in UX Guidelines, or about the decade the web spent learning to organize itself. School hands you tools, methods and critique; it rarely hands you the history that explains why the tools exist.

That gap matters, because the field is not a straight march of progress.

It is a stack of eras, each one solving the last and quietly inventing its own blind spot.

There are two famous lines about history, and UX earns both. George Santayana wrote that those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it. The version usually credited to Mark Twain is gentler: history doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. I like that one better.

This field does the rhyming kind. Each era makes a version of the same mistake in a new accent — it keeps the disposable habit and forgets the durable lesson that arrived with it. One thread runs through all of them, and it is worth naming up front. Economists refer to Jevons paradox: when something gets cheaper to produce, you don’t use less of it, you use far more.

Each time computing got cheaper — the personal computer, the browser, the smartphone, the design system — the work did not contract.

It expanded.

Truth in point — An Apple II in 2026 dollars would have set you back $14,300 ($2,638 original price). You can now pick up a MacBook Air for $1,099, at over a few hundred thousands times faster of the speed.

We went from computers that took up whole rooms to those we can fit in a pocket. It got more accessible, more people did it, and the industry grew.

Hold onto that, because the AI era is the same move at a larger scale, and the panic mistakes it for the opposite.

One idea outlasts every era, and it sets the bar. In a 2003 New York Times profile of the iPod, Steve Jobs pushed back on the idea that design is painting the house: design, he said, “is how it works,” not how it looks.

That is the durable lesson sitting under all five eras. Each one either remembers it or quietly trades it back for the surface.

So here‘s user experience in five eras, with rough dates, what each got right, and what each left you holding that you should put down. This is not nostalgia. Other histories slice the same decades differently — by interface paradigm, by platform, by tool — and those cuts are just as valid; this one is organized around the lesson each era kept and the habit it should have dropped.

The era you are in rewards the people who can tell the durable lessons from the expired ones.

The Human Factors Era (1940s–1988)

Before the screen, there was the system. Karlin’s group at Bell Labs shaped the touchtone keypad layout you still use today, working from how human hands and memory behave rather than from what was easy to build.

R. L. Deininger’s 1960 study tested circles, arcs, and two-row arrangements before the three-by-three grid won — it tested fastest, and people read the digits most naturally running left to right, top to bottom.

The founding insight of the whole field: you design around the person, not the machine, always.

The era is full of small decisions that quietly outlived it.

The hamburger menu is one — Norm Cox drew those three stacked lines in 1981 for the Xerox Star, and four decades later we’re still arguing about them in bars.

The language caught up slowly. Brenda Laurel used the phrase “user experience” in a 1986 essay, well before it was anyone’s title.

Don Norman coined it for his group at Apple in 1993 — the first person to carry the term in a job title — and he meant something wide: industrial design, graphics, the interface, the physical interaction, even the manual. The whole experience. Not the screen.

Norman’s word was never about screens. We made it about screens because screens were the part we could control.

What It Got Right

Experience is the entire system a person touches, not the rectangle they tap. Karlin’s team designed around hands and memory; Norman drew the term wide enough to hold the hardware, the interface, the interaction, even the manual.

The founding definition was expansive on purpose, and at its best the field kept that whole picture in view instead of retreating to the part that was easiest to control.

What It Got Wrong

Over the following decades we narrowed that definition down to flows and pixels, because pixels were the part designers owned. Now the rectangle is dissolving into voice, agents, and ambient interaction, and the narrow version leaves you designing the one part of the experience that is disappearing.

Today you can read the cost off the org chart: design owns the screen, while the model’s behavior, the data, and the policy get decided in rooms it was never invited to.

Pioneers

  • John E. Karlin, the first psychologist hired at Bell Labs to design how people use systems
  • Douglas Engelbart, who demonstrated the mouse and interactive computing in 1968
  • Jef Raskin, who started the Macintosh project around the human interface
  • Bruce Tognazzini, Apple employee #66, who wrote the first Apple Human Interface Guidelines in 1978
  • Don Norman, who wrote The Design of Everyday Things (1988) and became the first person to hold a “user experience” job title, ever
  • Brenda Laurel, who used the phrase “user experience” in 1986

Key books

  • The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction — Stuart Card, Thomas Moran, and Allen Newell (1983)
  • Designing the User Interface — Ben Shneiderman (1987)
  • The Design of Everyday Things — Don Norman (1988)
  • Tog on Interface — Bruce Tognazzini (1991)

Typical devices

  • Switchboards, rotary phones, and the touchtone keypad
  • Aircraft cockpit instrument panels and early radar consoles
  • Mainframe terminals and teletype machines
  • Xerox Alto and Star workstations
  • The original Macintosh (1984)

The Web Era (1994–2007)

The web arrived with no map. Early sites were filing cabinets dumped on the floor, and the discipline that rescued them was information architecture. Card sorts, taxonomies, navigation schemes, Jakob Nielsen’s usability heuristics. For roughly a decade, the central question of the field was not how a page looked but whether a person could find anything on it.

The browser also made publishing nearly free, and the predictable thing happened: everyone made a website, and suddenly the world needed people who could organize them faster than it could train them. The job grew faster than anyone could fill it.

This is also when the work got a process — Kelly Goto’s Web Redesign: Workflow That Works gave a chaotic young field a repeatable way to plan, budget, and ship a site, and taught a generation to treat redesign as a discipline rather than a scramble.

Information architecture didn’t die. It went underground and waited for the machines to need it.

What It Got Right

This era taught designers that structure is the product. How information is organized decides whether anything is usable at all, before a single visual choice gets made. A beautiful site with a broken hierarchy is a broken site.

We argued about labels and parent-child relationships because those arguments were load-bearing — get the structure wrong, and no amount of polish on top of it saves the experience.

What It Got Wrong

Then we mostly stopped. As apps and design systems took over, IA got demoted from a discipline to a deliverable, then to a phase nobody had time for, then to a sitemap made once and never reopened. Structure never stopped mattering; it just stopped being visible.

Today the bill arrives: teams wiring up AI agents find no legible structure for a model to reason over, and rebuild, under deadline, the architecture they deleted a decade ago.

Pioneers

  • Jakob Nielsen, who codified usability heuristics and discount usability testing
  • Steve Krug, who distilled it all into Don’t Make Me Think (2000)
  • Jesse James Garrett, who mapped The Elements of User Experience and later named Ajax
  • Peter Morville and Louis Rosenfeld, whose polar bear book defined information architecture
  • Alan Cooper, who introduced personas and interaction design through About Face
  • L. Jeffrey Zeldman, who championed most of the web standards we live by today.
  • Kelly Goto, who turned web redesign into a repeatable workflow and championed design ethnography

Key books

  • Information Architecture for the World Wide Web — Peter Morville and Louis Rosenfeld (1998)
  • Don’t Make Me Think — Steve Krug (2000)
  • Web Redesign: Workflow That Works — Kelly Goto and Emily Cotler (2001)
  • The Elements of User Experience — Jesse James Garrett (2002)
  • About Face — Alan Cooper (1995)

Typical devices

  • Desktop PCs with CRT monitors, driven by keyboard and mouse
  • Dial-up modems giving way to early broadband
  • Web browsers: Mosaic, Netscape, Internet Explorer
  • Palm Pilot and the first PDAs
  • Public information kiosks

The Mobile Era (2007–2014)

The iPhone shipped in 2007 and handed the field a constraint it had never had: a screen the size of a playing card and a person using it one-handed on a moving train.

You could not fit the desktop in there. You had to choose.

It also put a computer in nearly everyone’s pocket, which is where the thread from the intro shows up again. Computing got cheaper and smaller, so far more people used it, and the demand for designers who understood touch and mobile exploded.

The constraint even resurrected old ideas: the hamburger menu, dormant since the Xerox Star in the 1980s, came roaring back, because three stacked lines were the most economical way to hide a menu on a tiny screen. A decision made in 1981 became the default for a billion phones — not because it was beloved, but because the new scarcity made it useful again.

The phone made you choose. Take the phone away and most designers stop choosing.

What It Got Right

This was the most clarifying decade the field has had. Constraint forced focus. One primary action per screen. Progressive disclosure. Cut the secondary, hide the tertiary, kill the rest.

Designers learned to defend a single decision against a roomful of stakeholders who all wanted their feature above the fold, because there was no fold left to fight over. Scarcity did the editing, and the work got sharper for it.

What It Got Wrong

Then the constraints relaxed. Screens got bigger, scroll went infinite, compute got cheap, and the discipline the small screen imposed quietly evaporated.

We went back to cramming.

Constraint was never supposed to come from the device; it was supposed to come from the designer. AI removes the last hard one, the cost of producing the work, so nothing external forces the cut anymore. Today you see the result in interfaces bloated with everything the model could generate, because nothing in the tooling says no.

Pioneers

  • Scott Forstall, who led the software that became iOS
  • Jony Ive, whose industrial design set the hardware language
  • Luke Wroblewski, who argued the case for Mobile First (2011)
  • Josh Clark, who wrote Tapworthy and pushed designing for touch

Key books

  • Tapworthy: Designing Great iPhone Apps — Josh Clark (2010)
  • Mobile First — Luke Wroblewski (2011)
  • Responsive Web Design — Ethan Marcotte (2011)
  • The Lean Startup — Eric Ries (2011)
  • Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products — Nir Eyal (2014)

Typical devices

  • The iPhone and the capacitive multitouch screen
  • Android phones and the app-store model
  • The iPad and the first wave of tablets
  • Early fitness wearables such as Fitbit

The Design Systems Era (2014–2022)

Figma, tokens, component libraries, design ops as a job.

This era industrialized the parts of the work that repeat. The idea was older than the tooling, though: erin malone founded the Yahoo! Pattern Library (2004–2008), the first corporate pattern library published publicly, and the 2014 wave largely gave her team’s approach better tools and a budget line.

Instead of redrawing the same button forty times, you defined it once and propagated it everywhere.

The gains were real and measurable, if mostly self-reported: Figma’s own write-up credits Headspace with 20 to 30 percent time savings on routine tasks and Swiggy with halving feature rollout — vendor numbers, so read them as such. Independent work points the same way: in a controlled Sparkbox study, developers timed building the same form from scratch and then with IBM’s Carbon system, and the system produced faster, more consistent code, though the team was candid about the small sample.

The thread holds here too. Making design cheaper to produce did not shrink design teams; it let companies ship more product across more platforms, which meant more screens, more surfaces, and more designers to tend them.

Cheaper production bought more product, not less work. The design system was the factory, and the factory ran hot — right up until the next cost collapse arrived and changed what the factory was even for.

Process was insurance against the cost of getting it wrong. When the cost of getting it wrong drops, the insurance becomes overhead.

What It Got Right

Systematize the repeatable so you can spend your judgment on the parts that actually need it. Define the button once, propagate it everywhere, and stop relitigating settled decisions.

The gains were measurable — faster builds, fewer inconsistencies, less redundant work — and the discipline of naming and reusing components was a real advance. Components are good. Consistency at scale is good. None of that is in dispute.

What It Got Wrong

What is in dispute is everything that grew up around the components — the ceremony, the handoff rituals, the choreography of approving a screen. It made sense when execution was slow and expensive.

But execution is collapsing toward free in the world of AI, and the ritual that once guarded against costly mistakes is now just a tax on every decision.

Today the cost shows in the gap between teams: some ship in days, others take weeks to approve an undisputed button.

Pioneers

  • erin malone, who founded the Yahoo! Pattern Library (2004–2008), the first corporate pattern library published publicly
  • Brad Frost, who formalized Atomic Design
  • Nathan Curtis, who wrote much of the working theory of design systems
  • Alla Kholmatova, whose Design Systems (2017) gave teams a shared playbook
  • Matias Duarte, who led Material Design (2014)
  • Dylan Field and Evan Wallace, who built Figma into the era’s default canvas

Key books

  • Org Design for Design Orgs — Peter Merholz and Kristin Skinner (2016)
  • Atomic Design — Brad Frost (2016)
  • Design Systems — Alla Kholmatova (2017)
  • Expressive Design Systems — Yesenia Perez-Cruz (2019)

Typical devices

  • Responsive web spanning phone, tablet, and desktop screens
  • Standardized laptops and large external monitors as default kit
  • Smartwatches (Apple Watch, 2015)
  • Smart speakers and voice assistants (Amazon Echo, 2014)
  • Smart TVs and connected-TV interfaces

The AI Era (2022–Present)

Generative tools went mainstream fast. By 2025, generative AI adoption among US adults reached 54.6 percent, up ten points in a year, according to the St. Louis Fed. Inside companies the picture is more measured: the US Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey put firm-level AI use at roughly one in five through early 2026, and near 37 percent among firms with 250 or more employees.

That sits well under the louder headlines — self-selected commercial surveys tend to run two to four times higher, because they ask a broader question of a self-selecting crowd.

The cost of producing the work is falling toward zero, and the field is feeling it.

The UXPA salary survey found the worst net staffing reduction on its record, worse than the 2009 financial-crisis trough, with 37 percent of organizations reporting layoffs. The boom-time hiring of 2021 and 2022 has, by most readings, reverted to the mean.

Read that as a signal about the work, not a verdict on you. Here is the test of the thread: every earlier cost collapse grew the field, but this one so far looks like contraction. Jevons paradox says cheaper production should pull in far more work, and it may yet — but only for the part of the job AI can’t do, the way desktop publishing kept the editors and absorbed the paste-up artists. Drawing the screen is no longer where your value sits.

You are no longer the person who draws the screen. You are the person who decides what the screen is allowed to do.

What It Got Right

Here is where the whole history converges. The lesson the AI era is teaching, early and unevenly, is that the leverage moved upstream — to the rules, the structure, and the information the system reasons over.

That is the Norman lesson, design the system and not the rectangle, and the IA lesson, that structure decides whether any of it works, both returning at once. For the first time the two oldest insights in the field are also the most immediately useful.

And we almost forgot it.

What It Got Wrong

The first instinct was to bolt a chat box onto everything, then point the new tools at producing the same disposable screens faster — the oldest habit in a new coat.

Today you can spot it in products where the AI is a chat bubble stuck beside the old interface instead of rethinking it, and in teams measured by mockups shipped while the decisions that shape the experience happen in the prompt and the data. Stop counting mockups; start measuring the clarity of the structures the machine executes against. That was always the actual job.

Pioneers

  • Don Norman, still widening human-centered design to meet the moment
  • John Maeda, tracking where design and computation are converging
  • Josh Clark, arguing for “sentient design” built around AI’s capabilities
  • Amelia Wattenberger, prototyping what AI interfaces beyond the chat box could be

Key books

  • Designing Agentive Technology: AI That Works for People — Christopher Noessel (2017)
  • AI and UX: Why Artificial Intelligence Needs User Experience — Gavin Lew and Robert Schumacher (2020)
  • Conversations with Things: UX Design for Chat and Voice — Diana Deibel and Rebecca Evanhoe (2021)
  • uxGPT: Mastering AI Assistants for User Experience Designers and Product Managers — Patrick Neeman (2024)
  • Sentient Design: Crafting Intelligent Interfaces with AI — Josh Clark and Veronika Kindred (2026)

Typical devices

  • Conversational chat interfaces on web and mobile
  • Voice assistants and smart speakers as AI front ends
  • AI wearables: smart glasses and screenless pins
  • Headless agents that run with no device or screen at all
  • The same laptops and phones, now mediated through models rather than direct manipulation

What We Learned

Strip away the eras and the same shape repeats: each one handed the field a lesson worth keeping and a habit worth dropping, and the field reliably kept the habit. Here it is, era by era, so you can see which half you are still carrying.

Each one handed the field a lesson worth keeping and a habit worth dropping, and the field reliably kept the habit.

  • Human Factors taught that experience is the whole system a person touches, not the screen — then spent decades quietly narrowing that idea down to pixels and flows.
  • The Web proved that structure decides whether anything is usable before a single visual choice gets made, and then demoted information architecture to a phase you finish once and file away.
  • Mobile showed that constraint is what forces the clarity good work depends on, and promptly taught designers to wait for a device to impose it rather than generate it themselves.
  • Design Systems made the case for systematizing the repeatable so your judgment goes to the parts that need it, then wrapped the whole thing in a ceremony that only made sense while execution was expensive.
  • AI is teaching, unevenly, that the leverage lives upstream in the rules and structure the system reasons over — even as the reflex is still to measure your worth by the number of screens you can produce.
The first half of each line is a working definition of the job. The second half is what the next era charges you for holding onto.

Conclusion

Five eras, and one pattern underneath all of them: the field keeps the habit and forgets the lesson. The ledger above is the whole argument in miniature, and the uncomfortable part is how little of it is new. None of these lessons were waiting on better technology. They were waiting on us to stop treating each era’s convenience as a permanent rule.

There is a second thread, and it is the hopeful one. Cheaper production has grown this field every single time — the PC, the browser, the phone, the system each pulled in more work, not less.

The AI era can do the same.

But it removes the cover that let you carry dead habits along cheaply, so the growth will accrue to the designers doing the part the machine can’t, not the ones racing it to the bottom on output.

So the move is not to learn something foreign. It is to put down what you carry out of habit and pick up what the field already knew. The discipline has reinvented itself every decade since Bell Labs.

This is the first reinvention where the oldest lessons point the way out, and the only question is whether you reach for them before the next era makes you.

Five eras of UX design and the lessons to keep in the AI era was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: A short history of logos made of data
text:
A short history of logos made of data

An idea kept coming back in most branding projects I worked on in the past years: what if we embedded data in the logo? Real data, not symbols of information but information itself. Data that meant something for the client, that would shape the logo and create something unique. This idea came back again earlier this year and I knew I had to look deeper. So I spent time this summer searching for examples of logos embedding data: I went through graphic design books, online first (thanks to the amazing Internet Archive digital library) and in person in the beautiful reading rooms of the New York Public Library. Here is what I found.

First, there are a lot of logos out there, so let’s define what we’re looking for. Logo is simple: it’s the main mark for a brand. So no illustration, branded visuals or patterns. No data visualization that is not a logo, as iconic as it could be. Data is a bit harder: most logos carry meaning but very few carry data. So I found two questions that helped me make the distinction. First: does the data exist outside of the logo? Mercedes’ three-pointed stars symbolizes motorization on land, on water, and in the air. This is purely symbolic, not information. The second question: if the information changes, does the logo change? Here we can look at the Mexico City Metro logo by Lance Wyman: Wyman explains that his M logo is heavily inspired by the path of the first metro lines. One could almost use the logo to navigate the early metro system, but while that might have been true at some point, the system expanded a lot and the logo never changed. A great logo inspired by data but not a logo embedding data. So with these two questions in mind let’s start from the beginning.

Network

The oldest logo embedding data I could find dates from 1903. And while the word data itself might not be appropriate for its time, it definitely fits our definition. In the Bay Area in the early 1900s, while consolidating local streetcar lines under one company, the general manager realized that the overall shape of the network resembled “an old-fashioned key — three “handle loops” covering Berkeley, Piedmont and Oakland, a “shaft” formed by the ferry pier, and “teeth” representing the ferry berths at the end of the pier.” This simple shape, a stylized map, became their logo and their name: the Key Route. As the service expanded, the logo was redesigned as a flying key, and while the name and the key symbol remained, the ability to read the routes was lost. We went from a logo embedding data (the different streetcar routes) to a symbolic logo where the key was just an abstract reference to the past. In 1946 when the network was sold and buses were added the key entirely disappeared, remaining only in the company name.

I couldn’t find other examples from this time, but I have the intuition that this wasn’t the only company showing their network as part of their logo. I can imagine railroads or utilities using schematics of their early networks (not symbols of it, but the real schematics) as the most concrete sign of the company. Both helping their customers navigate the network and showcasing their imprint on the world.

Scientific Representation

The history of logos carrying data seems to follow the history of information design. While the development of railroad and utilities made network diagrams common, the 20th century brought to the general public the visual language of physics and chemistry. One notable logo from this time is the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) emblem. Designed in 1957 during the atomic age, it is a rare example of a logo evolving from symbolic to specific scientific representation.

Its first iteration displayed three orbits (representing electrons) orbiting a dot (representing a nucleus): the symbol of the atom. Not a specific atom, but the idea of an atom. A year later, someone at the agency noticed that it might not be the right logo for the IAEA: indeed the atom with three electrons is lithium, commonly associated with hydrogen bombs. Not ideal for the world’s “Atoms for Peace” agency reporting to the United Nations. A quick fix was proposed: adding an electron to turn it into beryllium. But in the process they also added dots for each electron and varied the orbit thicknesses. They turned a symbolic representation of the atom into an specific scientific visualization of beryllium. The final emblem was adopted in 1960, adding the blue color and olive branches from the United Nations.

In 2025, inspired by Mark Howarth’s protein alphabet, Leonora Martínez-Núñez created the logo for the Visualizing Biological Data international conference (VIZBI). The scientist turned professional scientific illustrator designed and animated each letter of the logo to represent the diverse topics discussed a the conference. My chemistry knowledge is extremely limited so take it with a grain of salt, but as the letters move away from the protein alphabet visualization they appear more abstract and symbolic, as if the logo was caught in the middle of a transition from specific protein visualization to a more abstract and general representation of chemistry.

From IAEA to VIZBI there is a tension between the symbolic representation and the scientific visualization. Fundamentally logos are signs, we don’t expect them to be accurate scientifically, but we expect them to be accurate symbolically. This can be resolved either by moving toward more symbolic and abstract representations, like the VIZBI logo, or by letting the specific representation function as a symbol, as shown by the history of the IAEA logo.

Charts & Graphs

With the advent of the personal computer, and later the internet, data took a more important place in our lives. Manipulating data became common in most office jobs, from very simple Excel spreadsheets to more complex analytics and visualizations tools. Data quickly became synonymous with information and control, a symbol of the computing era. It’s not surprising that in the early 2010s we see a series of logos showcasing data in its natural habitat: charts and graphs. A notable example is the 2013 logo for the Council on Australia Latin America Relations (Coalar) by the Australian agency Churchward/Melhuish. The logo combines the C from Coalar with a donut chart representing the land mass of Australia and Latin American countries. The largest ones like Brazil (green), Australia (yellow), or Argentina (blue) stand out while the smallest countries are shown at 1% of the land mass each. In a similar vein Open Knowledge logo, designed by Johnson Banks in 2014, combines two radial histograms showing how open data is in 72 countries. Both graphs (open in green, closed in red) form an O for Open.

But why stop at one dataset when the logo could evolve to show multiple? The 2015 APEC CEO Summit Philippines identity by Havas h2 encodes several datasets in different variations of the logos through radial bar charts. While it could be read as an abstract series of circular lines around its wordmark, everything is actually measured and plotted. The length of each line represents the main information: the default logo showcases GDP per capita, but other versions show population, land area (again), broadband or foreign investments among others. And their starting angle is plotted against the geographical location of each country, creating a series of unique charts.

Some logos push the abstraction further, bridging the gap between charts and data visualizations. Brand Bar (formerly Café Design) logo for Oppenheim law firm in Hungary is a good example: it takes the partners’ names, counts the frequency of each letter, and visualizes it in a unique radial shape. The result, one main logo for the firm and a series of unique ones for each partner, is quite beautiful and fully abstract: no legend, no explanation next to it, just a series of dots.

But all of these charts as logos are quite mysterious. They look like charts without legends, data without labels. One could say that unlike real charts these logos aren’t here to carry information but to convey the idea of information. And I would agree but I also think that what these logos truly want is to be deciphered. That creates an interesting tension: the data, while shaping the logo, only appears as a second layer that very few people will understand. “There is always that aha moment! ‘Oh so this is what this is telling us.’” comments the Chief Operating Officer of the APEC CEO Summit about the logo. To truly carry data, to fully serve their function, these logos need to be explained.

Dynamic

Around the same time, companies realized that data isn’t static numbers but rather massive information flows. One logo from the era stands out: the 2015 logo for Seagate by Goodby Silverstein & Partners. The data storage company’s rebrand was based on the idea of a “Living Logo”, showcasing “data as a living, vibrant thing that powers human invention, culture and advances”. Representing data storage isn’t easy and obviously Seagate doesn’t own the data it’s storing, so they partnered with Getty Images to turn its S monogram into an infinite flow of tiny images. The press release proudly explains that the logo can tell “an infinite number of visual stories about topics such as technology pioneers and breakthroughs in human history”. But the images are so small and there are so many of them, that their content (the data itself) doesn’t really matter. It’s impossible to tell what is shown here without zooming in (which an older version of the site apparently allowed). Again, this logo is about the idea of data rather than the specific data displayed. It’s about the quantity and the movement of data. There is something very 2010s in this logo, an optimism in technology and in infinite data feeds.

Designers realized that this logic can also be applied to design itself: a few parameters are enough to generate an infinite number of logos. They saw there an opportunity to explore new types of identities. As Irene Van Nes explains: a generative “identity can reflect the world it is living in, and adapt in response to its input.” But most generative identities don’t actually embed real data, they play with parameters without carrying information. One of the earliest generative identity based on real data I could find is the Visit Nordkyn logo by Neue Design Studio from 2010. The logo system is entirely driven by wind direction, wind speed and temperature from the Norwegian Meteorological Institute, updated in real time. The logo reflects how the weather influences life on Nordkyn, located in Norway’s northernmost county. 16 years later, it still lives on today, evolving every few minutes with the climate on Nordkyn.

Earlier this year, Base Design produced the visual identity for the 2026 Adelaide Biennial of Australian Art around a central element: Protocol, a programmatic typeface developed in collaboration with the foundry Counter Forms. The typeface mutates every 6 hours during the biennial, “driven by live environmental data: temperature, wind speed, surface pressure in Adelaide, and the S&P 500, a global barometer of financial markets.“ And “on the final day of the exhibition, the system reaches its programmed demise: bent, fragmented and exhausted.” The 109 iterations of the font are available for download here with the data source for each. Evolving following the font, the logo changed 109 times throughout the biennial. A fixed layout and yellow color made it recognizable, regardless of the typeface changes. In both logos, the data creates small variations around a main theme. Compared to Seagate, these logos are in a slow motion, one evolving every few minutes, the other every couple hours. They carry data at a slow pace, reflecting on time and their environment rather than on the speed of technology.

Beyond meaning and symbolism, dynamic logos are very hard to use as logos. Their dynamic nature is in direct contradiction with the reality of how logos are displayed: from physical such as engraved on hard drives for Seagate or printed on large exhibition posters for the biennial, to digital where social media platforms don’t allow profile pictures to be animated. So they need to be stabilized, frozen in their motion, stopped in a static state to truly exist. Ironically, I can’t show them animated in this article either. Most people will never experience their data flowing.

Cartographic

120 years after Key Route, cartographic logos are more common. And since I started researching for this piece a question stuck with me: are map based logos embedding data? Maps are a series of data points (coordinates) represented in a 2D space, so any logo including a map is by definition embedding data. But looking at probably the most famous map logo — the United Nations Emblem from 1946 — I’m having doubts. How far can you simplify a map before it’s not a map anymore? I’m not sure, but I know two logos that were recently released that might help us understand.

The first one is the Saaristo logo by Bond from 2025. Saaristo is an archipelago in Finland made out of 40,000 islands. The designers picked 8 whose shape resembles the letters of the word Saaristo. They printed and meticulously redrew the islands outlines creating a unique wordmark. Beyond the neat idea of a logo shaped by the place it represents, I think what makes it beautiful is that the rugged contours convey the scale of the islands and the natural elements shaping them such as wind, water and ice. Beyond data points, it makes us feel these islands.

Earlier this year, FutureBrand presented a new identity for The Brazilian Amazon with the goal of creating a unified destination brand for a very diverse region of 28 million inhabitants. At the core of the region, and its identity, is the Amazon river. Looking at the twists and turns of the river they got inspired and created a full alphabet. The Amazonia logo flows, from one part of Brazil to another. But unlike Saaristo, each shape has been freely redrawn, most probably to improve legibility and visual balance. This is a great logo, very clearly inspired by the shape of the river, but it’s a stretch to say that it carries data.

From Norway, to Finland, and Brazil, tourism logos are heavily represented here, as if embedding data grounded logos into the places they promote. As if embedding data allowed logos to carry a piece of these places with them.

To conclude let’s look at the ancestor of modern logos: heraldry. While coats of arms are neither logos nor what we’d call data, they are interesting to look at in this context. At a glance, heraldic signs feel very symbolic, built around specific rules and a limited number of patterns and colors, akin to today’s generative logos. But looking at it a bit longer reveals that it’s more complicated. Today’s historians agree that most of the symbols used are actually arbitrary identifiers. And some actually encode data. For example cadency is a system identifying descendants in a family. In England the first son is represented by a label of three points, the second by a crescent and so on, one symbol for each son. And the heir drops the label when the father dies. The mark literally updates when the information changes. For those who can decode them, coats of arms truly embed real world information. Data is encoded into some of oldest signs we have around us.

I wanted to write this short history because in all the books cataloging logos I could find, data didn’t seem to be a category. For example Yasaburo Kuwayama’s Trademarks and Symbols from 1973 sorts more than 3000 logos into visual subjects — what the logo depicts. And more recently plenty has been written on generative logos — how the logo is created. But nothing on what the logo encodes. For more than a hundred years, beyond meaning, logos have embedded information and I think it’s time to look at it as a proper category.

Sources

  • Per Mollerup, Marks of Excellence
  • Irene Van Nes, Dynamic identities : how to create a living brand
  • Yasaburō Kuwayama, International Logotype
  • Yasaburō Kuwayama, Trademarks & symbols
  • Jens Müller & Julius Wiedermann, Logo Beginnings Logo Modernism

title: How A Fashion Writer Styled Tennis Outfits For Her First US Open
text:
How A Fashion Writer Styled Tennis Outfits For Her First US Open

From my first-ever in-person tennis match to my first Honey Deuce cocktail, this year’s US Open brought a lot of exciting firsts for me. But before I even stepped into the Billie Jean King National Tennis Center, I had to get into the sporty spirit with my outfits. Because if Naomi Osaka and Aryna Sabalenka were serving (both in looks and on the court) in hooded capes and chunky jewelry, I could dress up for the occasion too.

For spectators and fans, tennis outfits can be super fandom-forward (with some wearing their merch as soon as they purchase it on-site) or super Wimbledon-adjacent (yes, some even wear stilettos!). Everything goes, from preppy polo tops and sporty baseball caps to crisp white dresses and dazzling tennis bracelets. So taking inspo from Pinterest — and trying to channel even an ounce of Zendaya’s iconic Challengers press tour looks — I opted for matching sets, preppy accessories, and tennis ball-inspired greens for my two US Open days.

Ahead, see how I interpreted tennis style as a fashion writer attending the sporting event of the season. And get outfit inspiration if you’re going to watch parties or heading to Arthur Ashe Stadium yourself for the quarterfinals and beyond.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Tennis Outfit Inspo: Sporty Sets

On my first match day, I was invited to attend with Offline by Aerie, so I put together an athleisure look for the occasion, and a matching set was the perfect starting point. I loved this longline sports bra, which felt more like a crop top, and flowy shorts, which gave tennis skirt vibes. But to shield myself from the blazing sun and sporadic rain showers, I added a cropped white button-down for an extra preppy layer.

On to accessorizing, I paired a baseball cap (in collaboration with Offline and the U.S. Tennis Association Foundation) with a compact crossbody bag, though Offline also offers a bag that looks like a tennis skirt, which would also be on-theme! I stuck with my trusty Nike Cortez sneakers in limited-edition gingham, but think any checkered or Mary Jane sneaker is a cool, modern take on a standard tennis shoe. And of course, I had to get some merch when I was in the stadium, buying an adorable tennis ball and racquet keychain that quickly became my bag charm of the day.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Tennis Outfit Inspo: Go Green!

Ever since I dyed my hair copper, green has been my favorite color to wear, and it has quickly filled up my wardrobe. From Kelly green and emerald to lime and chartreuse, my closet was made for a tennis match. Inspired by the shades of tennis balls and courts, I went all out with a green striped skirt, bold sunglasses, crossbody bag, and printed silk scarf. And because I had the US Open during the day and a Havaianas party at night, I had to slip into Brazilian flag-colored flip-flops for it all.

For sporting events, crossbody bags are definitely the way to go, and a convertible one that can also be worn as a top-handle, shoulder, or belt bag is a major win. I cannot tell you how surprisingly versatile my chartreuse Kate Spade Duo bag actually is (or just how many compliments it got at the matches). To complement it, I tied my sold-out Old Navy x Christopher John Rogers polka dot-printed scarf around the strap. And if you want the same look, there are tons of green polka dot or tennis ball print alternatives online. And while I accessorized with sleek silver jewelry, including my Bulova watch, you just know I would’ve worn a green-faced watch if I owned one to go green to the max.

title: A Week In Norristown, PA On A $180,000 Joint Income
text:
A Week In Norristown, PA On A $180,000 Joint Income

Welcome to Money Diaries where we are tackling the ever-present taboo that is money. We’re asking real people how they spend their hard-earned money during a seven-day period — and we’re tracking every last dollar.

This week: An office manager working in construction who makes $70,000 per year and spends some of it on a short bob cut.

If you’d like to submit your own Money Diary, you can do so via our online form. We pay $150 for each published diary. Apologies but we’re not able to reply to every email. We are legally unable to publish any diaries that have been written with the use of AI.

This diary was written in 2026.

Interested in taking our latest Money Diaries survey? We’d love to hear your thoughts here.

Occupation: Office manager
Industry: Construction
Age: 40
Location: Norristown, PA
Salary: $70,000
Joint Income/Financial Setup: $180,000. My husband and I have a joint checking account, HYSA, and cash back credit card. We also have our own personal checking, savings, and our own credit cards. We mostly use the joint credit card for expenses and bills to get cash back when we can. My husband contributes $686 a week to the joint checking, and I transfer $950 twice a month, sometimes more. My husband contributes more since he makes more than me, but since I have fewer bills than he does, I end up contributing extra.
Assets:
High-Yield Savings Account: $30,200
Combined retirement accounts: $172,230 (total across all of our accounts) Joint checking: $1,876.46
Debt:
New car: $18,300
My husband’s student loans: $12,000
Joint credit card: $2,734
Paycheck Amount (bi-weekly): $2,074, after 401(k)
Pronouns: She/her

Monthly Expenses

Housing Costs: $2,300 (my husband and I rent a two-bedroom single-family home)
Electricity: ~$200 for the warmer temps
Internet: $99
Gas: $225
Water: $70
Loan Payments:
Car payment: $368
Husband’s student loans: $500 (sometimes he pays more if he can)
Other:
Car insurance: $221
Cell phone: $225
Subscriptions: HBO Max: $20; Netflix: $19; Apple TV: $14; Reddit: $7; Spotify: $13; Peacock: $8.50; Amazon Prime: $16
Pet supplies: $130
Husband’s Personal Expenses:
Gym memberships & personal trainer: $350
My Personal Expenses:
Apple Music: $12
Clothing subscription: $98
Savings contribution: $700

Was there an expectation for you to attend higher education? Did you participate in any form of higher education? If yes, how did you pay for it?
Yes — my parents did not go to college, so there was an expectation. However, it was not strictly required that I go to college. I went to art school for undergrad, where I received several academic and housing scholarships, took out $15,000 in student loans, and my parents helped with off-campus housing expenses. I also went to graduate school, which my full-time job paid for 60% of, and the rest I paid for through $12,000 in loans.

Growing up, what kind of conversations did you have about money? Did your parent(s) educate you about finances?
My parents didn’t really educate me about finances. My parents did set me up with a checking account when I got my first job at 16. Then at 18 they set me up with my first credit card (which I still use!) that I used for college expenses, and my dad paid it off while I was in school. Otherwise, I learned on my own how to budget my money.

What was your first job and why did you get it?
My first job was at TJ Maxx, the chain retail store, at the age of 16. I got it to earn extra money to buy things for myself. My mom was a stay-at-home parent, and my dad was our primary income source. When I would come home from college for the summer, I would go back to TJ Maxx and work to save money for college expenses.

Did you worry about money growing up?
A little bit. I knew that my dad made a good amount of money for me, my brothers, and mom, but since he works in the construction world, there were times we couldn’t afford certain larger purchases. As I got older, I became more mindful of the costs of the things I requested from my parents. We would bargain shop a lot with coupons or find deals.

Do you worry about money now?
I think everyone worries about money to a small degree. I struggled through my late 20s and early 30s living solo on a small paycheck, and worried about money A LOT. I reached a point where I had no money, maxed out my credit card, and had to move back in with my parents. But now, I feel comfortably stable about being able to pay for monthly expenses, contribute to savings, and also be able to enjoy a few luxuries in life.

At what age did you become financially responsible for yourself and do you have a financial safety net?
When I was 24 years old, I moved out of my parents’ house after returning home from undergrad and was fully financially on my own. Now at the age of 40, my husband and I do have a financial safety net. His parents were in the medical field, and his dad made a very decent living. If something were to happen, I know my in-laws would step in to help. My husband and I also have four months of expenses saved in the event one (or both of us) lost our jobs.

Do you or have you ever received passive or inherited income? If yes, please explain.
I received inherited income from my grandmother. Before she passed away, my mom had power of attorney and gifted $10,000 to each of my grandmother’s six grandkids. She passed right after I graduated with my bachelor’s degree, so I used most of the money to buy my first car, which I had for 18 years.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day One: Saturday

6:00 a.m. — My alarm goes off and I take my daily birth control pill. I lay in bed a little bit longer as I didn’t sleep well last night and tossed and turned from 2:30 a.m. onwards. My husband, B., was also up around 2:30 and had gotten back in bed around 4:30. Both of us are out of bed by 6:30 and B. makes some coffee for us while I feed the cat breakfast. I take my coffee with oat milk and B. likes his black. I then turn on the TV to catch up on my weekly shows. We love food, so we have been watching Stanley Tucci: Searching for Italy.

7:15 a.m. — B. makes breakfast for me — scrambled eggs and an English muffin with peanut butter. He’s going for a bike ride soon, so he’s not having breakfast now. B. also cooks most of our meals since he used to be a professional chef — lucky me! I cook dinner on Wednesdays and Sundays.

10:35 a.m. — B. goes to the grocery store since I have to leave soon for my hair appointment. He gets kombucha, apples, bananas, carrots, greens, cucumber, oat milk (for me), chicken, ground turkey, chicken sausage, yogurt, macaroni and cheese, granola bars, Chex Mix and Fritos (for me), seltzer, and stuff for dinner (basil, mirepoix, ground meatloaf mix, ricotta, marinara). We use a shared grocery list app on our phones, and earlier I added items I need and most of our staples. Before shopping, we go on the GIANT grocery store app and clip any coupons. At the store, B. scans his reward card for $1 in grocery dollars, then with the coupons and discounts, he saves us an additional $14.72. $110.54

11:00 a.m. — I quickly eat a leftover slice of pizza from dinner last night before I jump in my car to head to my haircut and color appointment, which is at 12:15 p.m. I get my hair done about once every three months. On the way, I stop to get gas ($46.96), then I pop by FedEx to drop off packages for work. (I had prepaid labels on them already). $46.96

3:15 p.m. — I’m done with my hair appointment. I get highlights and a women’s cut. I went blonder this time since summer is approaching and got a cute, short bob cut. I’ve been with my stylist for a long time, so I give her and the shampoo girls a nice tip. $285

4:40 p.m. — I get back home and B. has washed our towels and the bedsheets! He has dinner in the oven, which is a fancy pasta dinner of stuffed shells. He bought this Italian pasta, Pastificio Di Martino, after watching an episode of Stanley Tucci: Searching for Italy last week, so he’s using the large shells — conchiglioni rigati from Campania, Italy. I pour myself a glass of white wine and sit outside on an Adirondack chair, enjoying the warm weather until dinner is ready.

Daily Total: $442.50

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Two: Sunday

7:00 a.m. — B. makes breakfast for us. He makes a frittata with broccoli, peppers, goat’s cheese, and basil, with fancy olive oil drizzled on top. B. and I were both up at 4 a.m. this morning for no reason.

8:45 a.m. — We leave the house for the day to head to the shore to spend some time with my in-laws. They just came back from being in Florida for six months. On the way, we pick up Starbucks. I get an iced grande caramel macchiato and B. gets an iced coffee. We also pop by my friend’s house to check in on their cats. $10.07

10:45 a.m. — We make it to the shore! (Tolls cost us $9.60 to get here). We catch up with my in-laws for an hour — we help bring up the flowers and soil for the deck planters that my mother-in-law purchased. There’s not much at the house to eat yet, so B. and I go to Chipotle and get chicken bowls ($25.96). $35.56

5:00 p.m. — We sit down to eat dinner that B. has cooked. He always cooks for everyone when we are at the shore house. We leave right after dinner to head home since it takes us an hour and 45 minutes to get home. We take the cheaper toll route home ($8.37), otherwise, it would cost us $18! $8.37

7:00 p.m. — When we get home, I feed the cat his wet food and we prepare for work the next day. I notice that the cat’s dry food is low, so I order it separately from his recurring order. $31.73

Daily Total: $85.73

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Three: Monday

6:00 a.m. — My alarm goes off and I take my pill. I really don’t want to get out of bed and go to work. I hit the snooze button at least three more times and then finally get out of bed at 6:30. I shower and get ready for work to be out the door by 7:40.

8:00 — I make coffee at the office. I brought my own oat milk and leave it in the work fridge. I don’t usually eat breakfast during the week, but I end up eating the snack I brought.

11 a.m. — Today has been a chaotic mess at work. I spent the morning rescheduling meetings; there was a homeless guy outside the building bothering people, a spam number kept calling the office number (which I answer), and then the clothing company across the hall accidentally had 30 boxes delivered using our office suite number. I had to meet the FedEx driver and get him access to the loading dock, which caused me to miss my boss’s messages regarding the rescheduled meetings. When I finally checked the FedEx packages, I realized every box was actually for the company across the hall. Needless to say, I wasn’t thrilled with them. 

1:45 p.m. — I finally sit down to eat lunch. I brought a salad I made from home: greens, carrots, cucumber, hummus, chicken, a boiled egg, and some homemade dressing.

5:40 p.m. — Home from work and B. has dinner almost ready. He cooked sausage, broccoli, and macaroni and cheese. After dinner, I drive over to my friend D.’s house, which is nearby, to return her tree trimmer that we borrowed. I also stop at Walgreens to pick up my prescription refill. $18.31

Daily Total: $18.31

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Four: Tuesday

6:00 a.m. — As usual, my alarm goes off and I take my pill. I carry on with my usual morning routine.

8 a.m. — I arrive at the office, but no breakfast for me. I just have a coffee with oat milk.

11:30 a.m. — My coworker says she’s going to order from Wawa for lunch and asks if I want anything, so I order a breaded chicken Caesar wrap. I didn’t have time to pack lunch this morning, so this works out nicely.

11:50 a.m. — The order arrives and I eat lunch in the kitchen. I Venmo my coworker $10 for lunch.

12:15 p.m. — I’m back at my desk working because there’s so much to do. This Thursday we are having a baby shower for another colleague who’s having a baby girl. I handle most of the internal and external events for my company, so I’m pretty much on my own planning and preparing for this shower. $10

5:00 p.m. — On my way home from work, I stop at the grocery store to pick up some ingredients to make a few appetizers for the baby shower at work on Thursday. I only have a $200 budget for food and decorations for 20 people, so I decide to make a few dishes (in addition to ordering some things) to get more bang for my buck. The theme is ‘garden picnic’, so I decide to make deviled eggs, pasta salad, and a veggie tray. I pick up 1.5 dozen eggs, baby carrots, cucumber, peppers, orzo, feta, red onion, cherry tomatoes, hummus, lemonade, lemons, and a $25 Starbucks gift card for the game prize. They don’t have a few items I want, so I will have to go to the GIANT near work tomorrow. $52.83 (Expensed)

5:45 p.m. — I’m back home and B. has dinner cooking because he’s a great husband and he gets home before me most days. He’s making a ground turkey bowl with brown rice. After dinner, B. insists on boiling and peeling the eggs for the deviled eggs I want to make for the baby shower — such a good guy I got here!

7:00 p.m. — I pour myself a glass of wine after doing a few things around the house and put on Top Chef to relax. B. scheduled a swim lesson with a trainer for this Saturday, which he had to prepay for ($50). He’s training for a race that involves swimming, running, and biking. $50

Daily Total: $60

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Five: Wednesday

6:00 a.m. — Same alarm time and same routine for getting ready for work. No, I still don’t eat breakfast and I always make coffee at work.

11:45 a.m. — I order lunch from Grubhub and get a poke bowl. $21.30

12:30 p.m. — It arrives and I sit at the work kitchen table with my coworker and we eat our lunches.

1:00 p.m. — After lunch, I head to the GIANT near work to get a few things for the baby shower that I couldn’t get last night. They have Martinelli’s Sparkling Blush and frozen raspberries that I need. $21.06 (expensed)

5:25 p.m. — I’m home from work and B. has already ordered Mexican takeout for dinner. Today is usually my day to make dinner, but I have to make deviled eggs and pasta salad for tomorrow, which is why we decided to order takeout. A. orders three chicken tacos, I get a massive burrito, and we split a churro. $53.28

6:25 p.m. — As I wrap up eating my burrito, B. brings in a FedEx package and just looks at me. I know what it is. My birthday is in a week’s time and he was teasing me on Sunday that he finally bought my birthday gift. I immediately open it and it’s a Kindle Scribe! I’ve been reading more lately since I joined the book club at work. I can also use it when traveling to keep notes on my crochet and knit patterns, too. After all that excitement, I start making the pasta salad and deviled eggs.

Daily Total: $74.58

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Six: Thursday

6:00 a.m. — My alarm goes off and it’s hard to get out of bed this morning. I get up a little earlier than usual since I have to pack everything I’m bringing to work for the baby shower, which is today!

8:00 a.m — I arrive at work and make my coffee with oat milk as usual. No breakfast for me, but I do have a mini blueberry muffin that my coworker brings in.

12:15 p.m. — I run out around lunch to pick up the tomato pie, the pretzel nugget tray, and a last-minute BJ’s Wholesale Club order for work. The pretzels and BJ’s order are prepaid with the company card, but I have to pay cash for the tomato pie. It’s the best in our area! $20 (Expensed)

1:05 p.m. — On my way back to the office, I stop and get gas in my car as my tank is really low. Gas has been high lately — it’s $4.51 per gallon at the Liberty Gas Station I go to, which is low for my area. $51

1:20 p.m. — I get back to the office and a coworker helps me unload everything. I also eat the salad I packed for lunch as I’m starving.

2 p.m. — I start setting up for the baby shower.

6:30 p.m. — The work baby shower was a hit! I’m exhausted, though. I’m finally home, waiting for B. to finish dinner. While waiting for dinner, I buy a case for my new Amazon Scribe ($24.47).

8:00 p.m. — I relax for the rest of the night until bedtime. (B. also got gas in his car today after work ($31.58)).

Daily Total: $107.05

DashDividers_1_500x100

Day Seven: Friday

6:00 a.m. — I’m alive! My alarm goes off as usual and I start a new pack of pills.

7:30 a.m. — I leave for work around 7:30 and say goodbye to B. and our cat. B. works remotely on Fridays — lucky him! On my way, I treat myself to some Starbucks. I get my usual grande caramel macchiato with oat milk and a bacon/gouda sandwich, too. $11.66

12:25 p.m. — Since this weekend will be Memorial Day Weekend, my work gives us a half day, in addition to Monday off — yay! I finish a few things, then check to see who is left in the office before locking the doors.

1:00 p.m. — I get home and B. is still on the couch where I left him, attempting to work. I brought him a couple slices of leftover tomato pie. I order some sushi for lunch since we don’t have much in the house. I’m really hungry, so I get a shrimp tempura roll, salmon roll, gyoza, and shrimp shumai. $40

2:45 p.m. — B. goes to the grocery store to get stuff to make pulled BBQ chicken for my parents’ Memorial Day Party and a few items for us to get through the weekend: hot dogs, buns, potato salad, kombucha, mac and cheese, bananas, kiwis, Chex Mix, onions, four packs of chicken, chicken stock, Sweet Baby Ray’s, and frozen pizzas ($109.26). While he’s gone, I preorder cannolis to bring to a housewarming we are attending on Saturday. $109.26

5:40 p.m. — B. makes the frozen pizzas for dinner. I pour myself a glass of wine.

7:00 p.m. — After dinner, I order yarn to fix my aunt’s crochet blanket I made her a couple of years ago ($19.06). Her puppy put a hole in one of the granny squares, which damaged mostly the yellow rows. Of course, I don’t have any of that yarn left. I end up finding it on an online website and then have to pay almost $10 for shipping. So much for fixing it before I see my aunt on Sunday! $19.06

Daily Total: $179.98

DashDividers_1_500x100

The Breakdown

Conclusion:
This was a unique week that included events and purchases that aren’t standard in an average week for me. I did spend more than usual, but a few expenses were reimbursed from work. After writing this Money Diary, I realized that most of our purchases are food-related. It doesn’t surprise me because my husband and I love food, and he used to be a chef and loves cooking. I do want to order less takeout for lunch in the future, though. I used to have better habits when it came to bringing lunch to work, so I would like to get back to that. I had a lot of fun writing this Money Diary and would definitely do it again!

title: How Amy Liu Built Her Sensitive Skin Brand Tower28 at 40
text:
How Amy Liu Built Her Sensitive Skin Brand Tower28 at 40

Before Amy Liu built Tower28, the company that currently sells products every 10 seconds in Sephora, she was working in the beauty industry and struggling with sensitive skin. With encouragement and investments from close friends, Amy leveraged her 15+ years of experience to bet on herself and build Tower 28, a company that keeps sensitive skin at the core of its product development. During the conversation, Amy shared that she dealt with chronic eczema and sensitive skin her entire life. However, despite working in major roles at companies like Kate Sommerville and Josie Maran and having firsthand experience of how product efficacy could change her life, she still didn’t feel ready to leap. Shortly after turning 40, Amy was in conversation with a former business school classmate who asked what she was waiting for. This friend affirmed her skills and experience, and then offered to invest in her dream. She reached out to other friends and family, all of whom were excited to support her vision for Tower 28. In the seven years since launching, Tower 28 has blossomed into a brand beloved by everyone from essential workers to “gym rats,” to celebrities, and influencers like Hailey Bieber and fellow Naked Beauty guest, Toni Bravo. Amy offers us a glimpse into her life as CEO, mom, and lifelong advocate for clean beauty in this chat. She shared what it was like growing up in Los Angeles, in a predominantly white community, instead of a Chinese-American neighborhood.

During the episode, Amy details her parents’ decision to move to America and why her dad, an entrepreneur, tried to dissuade her from starting a business. It’s exactly this persistence that has allowed her to become a strong leader, despite having been exposed to some of the worst bosses you might imagine. Amy’s leadership skills are defined by not only what she has done but also by her commitment to educating others. In the summer of 2020, she decided to develop Clean Beauty Summer School, a professional-development program that gives BIPOC founders industry access and education that they might otherwise not have access to. Amy has built a brand that is 100% compliant with the National Eczema Association and regularly gives back to minority founders. Amy Liu’s story proves that a true commitment to inclusivity benefits every single one of us.

title: Venus In Scorpio Is Here — & You Shouldn’t Make Any Impulsive Moves
text:
Venus In Scorpio Is Here — & You Shouldn’t Make Any Impulsive Moves

From September 10th to October 25th, Venus enters Scorpio — and it’ll be a vibe. Take note because it’s all-or-nothing energy can consume us, encompassing a deep, passionate love affair with others, ourselves, and the world. There is nothing or no one that Venus in Scorpio leaves unchecked in its path towards finding commitment, which is why we hold it in high regard. On occasion, Venus in Scorpio can be possessive and hold grudges because the Water sign does have stingers that it takes out when people upset it. However, most of the time, this placement wants to connect with others and has a fierce aura that changes our lives for the better. 

This year, Venus in Scorpio is experiencing an interesting turn of events, due to the retrograde it’s undergoing from October 3rd to November 13th. Let’s start with the aspects it’s making to the healing centaur Chiron, add evolutionary Pluto (the modern planetary ruler of Scorpio), and action-oriented Mars (Scorpio’s traditional planetary ruler), and we have a mix of intense energy shaking up the mood. 

Venus will oppose Chiron retrograde in Taurus on September 10th, asking us to look within ourselves to remedy situations, while reconciling our fears. The caveat is that we’ll seek validation from others, but we should look within ourselves for confidence. People will mirror our actions, forcing us to reassess how we treat them and ourselves. When Venus squares Pluto in Aquarius three times on September 15th, October 20th, and December 9th, desires will explode. Power struggles may persist. Venus and Mars in Leo create a whirlwind connection on October 10th (the day of the New Moon in Libra). These forces entice us to forge meaningful relationships that grow on December 12th, when Venus harmonizes with Mars in Virgo, laying down the foundation for our future.

Now, let’s jump into Venus retrograde! The moonwalk lasts 42 days, making the onset of cuffing season complex. Venus will be gliding backward in Scorpio from October 3rd to 25th, re-entering Libra from October 25th to December 4th. Then, Venus moves back into Scorpio from December 4th to January 7th, 2027. The pre-shadow period began on August 31st in Libra, and the post-retrograde zone ends on December 15th in Scorpio. December 29th is the time to DTR [Define The Relationship] because the Nodes of Destiny offer a choice in how we want to move partnerships forward — or not. 

Venus retrograde forces us to contemplate what we value and align with. In Scorpio, we’ll be looking at who we wish to be intimate with — not for now, but for the long run. We’re releasing anything that makes us question our intuition and merging with those that help us feel confident. The best days of the retrograde are October 6th and 23rd, when Mercury and the sun form a conjunction with Venus in the same sign and degree. They’re great moments to make decisions and plans for the future. Committing to a new relationship is not recommended when Venus is backstroking, so use those days to go out with friends and have profound conversations.  

Venus retrograde in Scorpio isn’t a time to commit to a new look. If you’re looking to make any changes to your style or ‘fits, put them on the board for later; you could always come back and reinvent yourself once Venus goes direct. 

Overall, Venus in Scorpio offers the opportunity to clear the air through introspection, prompting us to reevaluate our circumstances. We’re figuring out how to proceed in ways that are healthy and meaningful. It’s important to put ourselves first and listen to our gut feelings; don’t deny ourselves the sentiments that propel us in any direction. If we get lost in the mix or are moody at times, it’s totally fine. The transit’s complex nature will be a roller coaster, so hold on tight for the bumpy ride and don’t make impulsive moves — at least until Venus clears the post-retrograde shadow.

title: The New Moon In Virgo Is Here — & A Lot Of Change Is Coming Your Way
text:
The New Moon In Virgo Is Here — & A Lot Of Change Is Coming Your Way

Beware: The last New Moon of summer on September 10th is a doozy! The New Moon in Virgo, which marks the onset of the monthly lunar cycle, brings a lot of change our way. At this point, we’re probably tired of having to evolve and transcend every week — but the cosmos are prepping us for the onset of retrogrades that are happening in the fall. You know the drill…

The New Moon is triggered by Mars in Cancer, blending intuition with action. We’re going to find a way to integrate our internal emotions into how we pursue our desires and goals. The caveat is that our high energy and determination may make us super competitive with others, particularly those with whom we don’t wish to have conflict. In the end, we may not feel great about winning because the result distances us from people we care about. In Virgo fashion, we’ll blame ourselves when we should be mad at the circumstances. The lesson is that we can maintain friendships and alliances without escalating the issue.

The good news is that if we’re looking to start a project or take the lead at work, the New Moon’s connection to Mars gives us the stamina to do so. This isn’t a time to sit on the sidelines, even though we may not be emotionally ready to confront matters. Since the vibe can lead to passive-aggressive feelings, we intend to pursue endeavors and ventures that speak to our spirit. Under this cosmic influence, being direct is challenging, which is why underlying tensions can heighten. Beware of backhanded comments and attacks that appear out of thin air.

Taking the astrological influences of the sky further, Saturn retrograde in Aries forms a quincunx (or inconjunct) with the New Moon. This minor frustration pushes us to be cautious and pragmatic in how we move forward; although Mars is pushing us to react with wild sentiments, Saturn retrograde urges us not to let others get to us in that way. To handle the vibe, we must address matters maturely and offer simple responses. The objective is not to give others fuel to start a fire, but to have a chill demeanor in the face of adversity and not let their drama create problems in our lives. 

The presence of the fixed star Asterion (Chara) alludes to ruthless and selfish attempts to control outcomes. We can conquer our goals, but be at odds with our frenemies. Their success isn’t going to sit well with us; in fact, it might make us do shady stuff behind their backs to sabotage them — the same applies to their behavior. Protecting our energy is vital to ensure they stay in their lanes and don’t let their insecurities swerve into our auras. Even if we want to be of service and help others, we must think twice before intervening. We may find ourselves feeling a certain type of way (jealous or angry) as a result. 

The same day as the New Moon in Virgo, Mercury glides into Libra, Venus enters Scorpio, and Uranus retrograde in Gemini commences. These planetary shifts will pack a lot of punch, so it’ll be hard to keep up. Mercury’s movement into Libra is going to be pivotal, as the planet of communication rules Virgo. The verdict on how we wish to proceed will still be out, due to the indecisiveness of Mercury in Libra. Venus’ dive into Scorpio sets the tone for the next several months. 

The romantic planet, Venus, begins its retrograde on October 3rd, lasting until November 13th. Venus remains in Scorpio until January 7th, 2027, making the circumstances that are set forth on September 10th significant to the ongoing saga we’ll be facing. Uranus’ moonwalk in Gemini, which completes its cycle on February 8th, 2027, is eye-opening and reflective. Revolutionizing our lives is an uphill battle because we have to leave our comforts behind and do not want to. On the other hand, it brings us into the future, allowing us to advance and grow. 

All in all, the New Moon in Virgo is an extremely potent time. Tread lightly and focus on yourself. If you’re feeling daring, go out and have midnight margaritas or watch Practical Magic 2, to find out how you can enchant your life for the better.

title: Amelia Dimoldenberg  Reminds Us That Your Dream Job Doesn’t Have To Be Forever
text:
Amelia Dimoldenberg Reminds Us That Your Dream Job Doesn’t Have To Be Forever

After 12 years and thousands of chicken nuggets, Amelia Dimoldenberg has called time on her successful YouTube series, Chicken Shop Date.

With 3.4 million subscribers, over 1 billion views on YouTube, and 2.1 million followers on Instagram, what began as a column for Amelia’s local youth club magazine grew into one of the most popular celebrity interview formats on the press circuit.

The self-created series turned Amelia’s charming yet awkward British flirting into a compelling viral sensation and put her show at the top of every celebrity publicist’s press list.

In 2025, the host was named in Time Magazine’s TIME100 Creators list as one of the most influential digital content creators and has hosted the Academy Awards red carpet for the past three years.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Chicken Shop Date (@chickenshopdate)

On paper, the 32-year-old was at the top of her game. That’s why an Instagram post announcing the end of Chicken Shop Date came as such a surprise.

On Thursday, 3 September, Amelia wrote, “I never thought I’d stop Chicken Shop Date, I thought maybe it would be a part of me forever, and in some way it always will, but I feel like it’s now time to move on from this adventure and onto a new one.”

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Amelia Dimoldenberg (@ameliadimz)

Describing the show as her “very own romcom”, Amelia announced a slate of final dates before the beloved chicken shop closes forever.

While the news is sad (and we’ll all miss witnessing celebrities blush over Amelia’s signature deadpan charm), knowing when to say goodbye to a creative project is both a brave and strategic business move.

The millennial dream

As children, millennials were told they could be whatever they wanted to be. If we worked hard, applied ourselves and stayed on track, all of our dreams would come true. With elder millennials graduating into the 2008 Global Financial Crisis and zillennials graduating into a pandemic, it was also instilled in us that once you’re in the room — once you’ve “made it” — don’t ever let it go.

Exemplified by Emily Charlton’s “A million girls would kill for this job” line in Devil Wears Prada, if you were lucky enough to achieve your career dream in a climate of redundancies, cost of living pressures and stagnant wages, you should be grateful and grip onto it tightly.

But what happens when you’re ready for a new dream? For Amelia, the answer seems to be: you go for it. Through her own production company, Dimz Inc., Amelia has multiple creative opportunities in the works, including writing her own romcom film and a series in production for the BBC.

Chicken Shop Date isn’t the first example we’ve seen of a wildly successful creative project calling time while at its peak. In 2020, British pop culture podcast The High Low, hosted by writers Dolly Alderton and Pandora Sykes, called it quits after four years spent dominating the charts. The pair told Grazia UK that when they began the podcast they decided they’d be “all in” for four years.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Dolly Alderton (@dollyalderton)

“We wanted to go out on a high, and we feel like we’ve really honored the show by ending it now,” they told journalist Anna Silverman. Since ending The High Low, Dolly has gone on to publish her novel Good Material in 2023, write a Pride and Prejudice Netflix adaptation, and turn her memoir, Everything I Know About Love, into a TV series.

Pandora has created the UK’s number one culture newsletter, Books+Bits, and hosted multiple podcasts, including The Missing and Unreal: A Critical History of Reality TV for the BBC.

While the pair have gone on to work on other exciting things, there’s no denying that walking away from a creative and commercially successful project is daunting.

In a capitalist society, where success is measured by wealth and, increasingly, social media views, “quitting” a successful venture rejects the sunk-cost fallacy. But perhaps our idea of success should be ever-changing. We’re constantly told to dream bigger, but maybe the bravest thing you can do is admit that you’ve already achieved the dream — and start a new one.

I’m reminded of this as I sit in my therapist’s office explaining that the people I once aspired to work with are now my creative peers. How it’s so normal. The therapist suggests that, despite having achieved exactly what 24-year-old me wanted, maybe six years on I’m a bit… bored. Maybe, for this chapter, I’ve “made it”. She asks what a new dream could look like. It feels like a revolutionary statement, but she’s right. What was The Dream in your early 20s doesn’t have to be the same at 30.

Our culture teaches us to always strive for more: more money, more followers, more opportunities. But as Amelia has shown, it can be even more satisfying to close a chapter on your own terms rather than continuing on until the format stales or, as the internet is wont to do, Amelia gets “woman’d” (a phrase coined by culture writer Rayne Fisher-Quann for the cultural phenomenon where the internet stops liking a woman at the same time).

In a recent interview with Rolling Stone, Canadian musician Sarah McLachlan explained why she ended her music festival Lilith Fair after just three years. Between directing a festival, touring, songwriting, and recording albums, similar to Amelia, Sarah made a call on when to step back from a successful project.

“I like ending things on a high note,” Sarah shared. “It was also a selfishly motivated thing too, of ‘I’m sort of losing myself’ in this too much.”

It’s a sentiment Amelia seems to understand. With a movie and TV series already in the works, we know that the Chicken Shop Date host will go on to achieve other markers of traditional Hollywood success. But there’s no denying that it’s refreshing to see a woman create her own bootstrapped series, turn it into a cultural phenomenon, and then decide that this particular dream has run its course — even while it’s still at the top.
